summary:
PLANITIA is a web platform we built to plan safe, efficient rover and astronaut routes on Mars. It focuses on three candidate landing sites, AP-1, AP-8 and AP-9 in Amazonis Planitia, where research suggests there is ice just below the surface. The platform places Viking imagery and MOLA elevation data under a grid of 330 cells. Each cell gets a risk score from 1 to 5 based on slope, surface roughness and obstacles, temperature, and atmospheric pressure. Users pick from seven science targets, such as brain-coral terrain, expanded craters and polygonal ground. An A* algorithm then finds the lowest-risk path between them. PLANITIA estimates the route’s distance using Mars’s real radius and its travel time from a speed the user can change, and the finished mission plan can be exported as a JSON file.

Water ice is one of the most valuable resources for future human missions, but the terrain around it can be dangerous. PLANITIA brings published science and risk-aware route planning into one simple tool. This helps mission planners decide where to go and how to get there before anyone sets foot on Mars.
details:
What it does
PLANITIA is a web platform that plans safe routes for surface exploration around three candidate landing sites near the Martian ice deposits: AP-1 (the base of operations), AP-8 and AP-9. Users choose from seven science targets. These include brain-coral terrain, a ring-mound crater, a crater with exposed ice, bullseye and inverted expanded craters, and smooth and knobby polygonal terrain. PLANITIA then works out the lowest-risk route between them and estimates how far and how long the trip will be.

How it works

  • Map: the study area is shown on NASA’s Viking MDIM 2.1 color mosaic. Users can switch to a MOLA elevation layer.
  • Risk grid: the area is split into a 15 × 22 grid (330 cells). Each cell gets a risk level from 1 (very low) to 5 (very high) based on slope, surface roughness and obstacles, temperature, and atmospheric pressure.
  • Route planning: an A* pathfinding algorithm moves through the grid one cell up, down, left or right. Entering a cell costs 1 plus its risk level, so the route avoids hazards instead of simply taking the shortest line.
  • Distance: each route segment is measured with the haversine formula, which calculates distance on a sphere, using Mars’s mean radius of 3,389.5 km.
  • Time: travel time is the distance divided by a walking or driving speed the user can change (4 km/h by default).
  • Science cards: each target has a card explaining what might be found there, what to investigate, and the limits of the evidence, based on Luzzi et al. (2025) and Viola et al. (2015).
  • Mission sequence: users can reorder the stops, and the final plan can be exported as a JSON file.

Benefits
PLANITIA puts published landing-site science, real NASA imagery and elevation data, and risk-aware route planning in one tool that is easy to use. Planners can compare route options in seconds and see exactly why a path was chosen.

Intended impact
Water ice is essential for future human missions. PLANITIA helps answer two questions before launch: where crews should go, and how they can get there safely. It can also be used to teach students and the public how missions are planned.

Limitations
The distances are horizontal estimates, so they don’t include slopes or detours. The time estimates leave out rest stops and science work. The positions of targets P1–P7 still need to be checked independently.

Tools and data

  • NASA Mars Trek (Viking MDIM 2.1)
  • MOLA MEGDR elevation data, from the NASA PDS Geosciences Node
  • JPL planetary physical parameters
  • Luzzi et al. (2025), JGR Planets, DOI 10.1029/2024JE008724
  • Viola et al. (2015), Icarus
  • The original route algorithm, written in C++
  • Hosted on Netlify (planitia.netlify.app)
